task.name: A failure cause code is assigned from text describing the target repository's source rather than forge's own run
task.story_text:
## Observed

Observed in sprint issues-248,245,246,231, story #248.

Forge recorded the story's primary cause as unknown_needs_rca, meaning it had already
determined it could not classify the failure. It nonetheless attached a contributing
cause naming an unapplied fallback, and surfaced to the operator the next step "wire
the provider fallback so the next failure recovers automatically".

The evidence string attached to that contributing cause was a sentence lifted from
the story's own preflight log. That sentence described the target repository's
application code — a rest-timer scheduling function that invalidates a session
unconditionally with no fallback or guard path preserving the existing alarm. It was
an analysis of the defect the story existed to fix. It had no relationship to forge's
own fallback machinery, which is what the cause code denotes and what the
recommendation told the operator to go wire.

The classification therefore rested on a word appearing in a description of the work,
matched as though it were a description of the run. The operator-facing recommendation
that followed pointed at a subsystem that had not failed and was not involved, while
the actual failure went unexplained.

## Expected

A cause code should be assigned only from evidence about forge's own
execution. Text originating in the target repository — its source, its issue body, its
preflight analysis — describes the work being attempted, not the run attempting it,
and must not be matched into runtime cause codes on the strength of shared vocabulary.
When forge has determined it cannot classify a failure, that determination should
propagate: it should not also emit a confident contributing cause, and it should not
derive an operator recommendation from one. Recommending remediation of a subsystem
on unsupported evidence costs more operator trust than declining to guess.
## Diagnosis

- **Observed symptom:** the `provider_fallback_not_applied` rule fires on
  reviewer prose containing the phrase "no fallback", adding a false
  contributing factor and a false recommended action to a story's RCA entry.

- **Evidence:** the rule declares plain-English patterns —
  `patterns=("fallback not applied", "no fallback", "fallback unavailable")` at
  `src/theforge/sprint/rca.py:270`, within the rule defined at lines 265-271.
  Alphabetic patterns are matched as unanchored substrings: `_pattern_matches`
  (`src/theforge/sprint/rca.py:674-685`) anchors only purely-numeric patterns
  with digit boundaries and applies plain containment to everything else. The
  text scanned includes agent-authored content, because `_collect_text_sources`
  (`src/theforge/sprint/rca.py:592-671`) gathers the story's iteration logs and
  run log as sources. The false hit is recorded in
  `hdp/.forge/logs/issues-248,245,246,231/sprint-rca.yaml` under `issue-248`,
  citing `issue-248/preflight-raw.log`, and the corresponding action string is
  emitted by `_recommend_actions` (`src/theforge/sprint/rca.py:922-986`).

- **Ruled out:** not a mis-scoped source list — scanning agent output is
  deliberate and is what lets genuine text rules such as
  `worker_thread_timeout` and `provider_usage_limit` work; the defect is the
  pattern's specificity, not the corpus. Not a one-off phrasing coincidence —
  "no fallback" is unqualified ordinary English and will recur in any review
  discussing error handling, as will "rate limit" and "overloaded" in the
  `provider_usage_limit` rule, so the class of defect is structural rather than
  incidental to this run. Not a priority or precedence bug — the rule's
  `contributing` role is correct and it did not displace the primary class; it
  was wrong to fire at all.

- **Confirmed cause:** `provider_fallback_not_applied` is keyed on generic
  English phrases matched as unanchored substrings against natural-language
  agent output, so it cannot distinguish forge reporting that a provider
  fallback did not apply from an agent writing about fallbacks in the project
  under development.

- **Affected code path:** `src/theforge/sprint/rca.py` — the
  `provider_fallback_not_applied` rule (lines 265-271), `_pattern_matches`
  (lines 674-685), `_text_rule_hits` (lines 687-713), and the
  `fallback_not_applied` action string in `_recommend_actions` (lines 922-986).

- **Fix-success criterion:** an RCA generated over a run whose only occurrence
  of "fallback" is in agent-authored prose about the project under development
  records no `provider_fallback_not_applied` factor and no provider-fallback
  recommended action; and an RCA over a run in which forge genuinely declined or
  failed to apply a configured provider fallback still records it.

## Notes

The generalizable half is that a text rule keyed on ordinary English cannot be
made reliable by tightening the phrase, only by anchoring it to something forge
emits itself — a structured field, or a log line with a marker the coordinator
controls. `provider_usage_limit` (`rca.py:131-150`) carries the same exposure
with patterns including "rate limit" and "overloaded"; it was not observed
misfiring in this run and is not claimed as a defect here, but a fix that only
edits the fallback strings leaves the shape in place.

Diagnosis added 2026-07-29 while auditing whether `forge rca` would have surfaced
the real cause of the same sprint's failure. It did not, and this false positive
was in the same artifact.

handoff.summary: Converted the provider_fallback_not_applied RCA rule from unanchored English substring patterns ('no fallback', 'fallback unavailable', 'fallback not applied') to a field-derived signal rule detected in _fallback_not_applied_evidence, which reads the run's own dev-loop transport telemetry from the per-story audit: transport_fallback_reason set (a fallback-eligible CLI transport failure forge itself classified) with transport_fallback_fired false (no fallback transport ran). This is the fallback machinery reporting on its own execution, so agent-authored prose about the target repository can no longer assign the cause code on shared vocabulary. Separately, when the primary class is unknown_needs_rca, contributing factors whose evidence came only from a text scan are no longer promoted into contributing_factors and no operator recommendation is derived from them; their evidence entries are still recorded so the trace is not lost, and structured field-derived contributing factors (the run's own recorded facts) still stand. RULESET_VERSION bumped 4 -> 5 so the changed conclusions are a visible, versioned re-analysis; the two existing tests that pin that constant were updated to match (the monkeypatched 'improved' version in test_improved_ruleset_regenerates_versioned moved 5 -> 6). Added six tests including a coordinator-audit seam test driving real DevIterationTelemetry through generate_audit_log into the RCA engine, so the cause code is verified against the field the coordinator actually writes.

story_deviations: Expected section reads 'it should not also emit a confident contributing cause' when primary is unknown. I implemented this for text-scan-derived contributing factors only; contributing factors derived from forge's own structured audit/summary fields (dev/review iteration limits, and the new telemetry-derived fallback factor) still stand under an unknown primary. Rationale: those are the run's recorded facts rather than an inference from vocabulary, and suppressing them would discard real signal the operator needs precisely when nothing else explains the failure. A blanket suppression is a one-line change to the filter in _classify_story if the stricter reading is wanted.

RULESET_VERSION 4 -> 5 required editing two existing assertions in tests/test_sprint_rca.py (test_ruleset_version_stamped, test_improved_ruleset_regenerates_versioned) that pin the constant. These tests are directly about the version contract this change is obliged to bump; no test logic or coverage was weakened.
deferred_items: provider_usage_limit (rca.py:131-150) still carries the same structural exposure via 'rate limit' / 'overloaded' / 'resource exhausted' patterns matched against agent prose. The story's Notes explicitly scope it out as not-a-claimed-defect; the anchoring pattern established here (field-derived from forge-emitted telemetry, e.g. cli_quota_error_observed which the audit already records per dev iteration) is directly reusable for it.

handoff.summary: Iteration 2 (advisory cleanup after APPROVE) addresses the carried P2 on provider_usage_limit, which shared the exposure #2031 fixed for the fallback rule: 'rate limit', 'overloaded', 'resource exhausted' are ordinary English matched as unanchored substrings against agent prose. Rather than deleting patterns that still catch real provider errors nothing else records (API-transport quota errors appear only in captured output; cli_quota_error_observed is CLI-only), it gets two guards. First, a new RcaRule.forge_emitted_only field, set on provider_usage_limit and honored in _text_rule_hits: the rule's patterns are scanned only against sources forge emitted about its own run, never against 'authored'-kind sources (markdown and preflight artifacts, which carry analysis of the target repository). Second, a new _provider_quota_evidence signal so the rule fires field-derived from cli_quota_error_observed in the coordinator audit's dev-loop telemetry — forge's own classification of its own CLI invocation — with no text at all; it is restricted to the terminal dev iteration with no fallback fired, because provider_quota is the highest-priority primary class and promoting a quota blip that a later iteration or a fallback recovered from would send the operator to wait out a quota reset that was never the blocker. Extracted _dev_loop_entries so both telemetry readers share one guarded accessor. Iteration 1's work (fallback rule converted to field-derived; unknown_needs_rca dropping text-derived contributing factors and their recommendations) is unchanged and its tests still pass.

finding_registry.description: The provider_usage_limit rule matches generic English phrases like 'rate limit' and 'overloaded' as unanchored substrings against natural-language agent output, exposing it to false positives when agents discuss resource limits in the target repository.

soft: Coordinator is pure Python — no LLM calls for routing or process decisions
Schema validation is the integrity boundary — do not relax cross-validation rules
Keep modules single-purpose; extract instead of growing monolith files
Keep pure-data types in low-dependency modules with stdlib-only imports
Separate prompt construction, output parsing, and coordinator control flow

When adding or modifying data that flows between coordinator phases, instrument the change so the actual values are visible in the audit trail — diagnosing sprint failures requires tracing real data, not reconstructing it
Do not create files outside src/, tests/, or docs/. If you need a scratch file for exploration, delete it before committing.
